title: Print for the robot
summary: Design and print a working part for the mBot, a bumper or a sensor mount, iterate it once, and see how infill trades print time for strength.
materials: small paper cups and washers or pennies, for the strength test

figure.alt: The mBot's body is sketched with the point where the new part attaches marked at its bottom edge. The new bracket or bumper is drawn separately, positioned to fit against that same attachment point.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop continues: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: can a printed part earn its place on a working robot, not just sit on a shelf? A part that must actually survive a bump or hold a sensor steady has to be strong enough, not just the right shape.

Imagine: a bumper that softens a small crash, or a bracket that holds the ultrasonic sensor at a steady angle instead of wobbling. Either one has to fit the mBot's real screw holes and body.

Plan: measure where the part attaches to the mBot with the calipers, then sketch the part on graph paper with those measurements. Pick one setting to test three ways before printing the final version: infill, the amount of plastic filled in inside the part rather than left hollow.

figure.alt: Two cross-sections of the same part show the inside lattice at ten percent infill, sparse and quick to print but weaker, compared with fifty percent infill, a denser lattice that takes longer to print but holds more weight.

steps.title: Infill trades time for strength
steps.body:
A 3D print is rarely solid plastic all the way through. Most of the inside is a lattice, printed thinner or thicker depending on a setting called infill, usually written as a percentage of how much of the inside gets filled.

Low infill uses less plastic and finishes faster, since the printer skips most of the inside and only prints a thin skin. High infill packs the inside fuller, using more plastic and taking longer, but the extra material inside is what a part leans on when something pushes or bends it.

There is no single right infill. A part that only needs to look right and never carries weight can print quickly at low infill. A part that has to hold weight or survive a knock, like a bumper or a sensor mount, needs enough infill to actually be strong. That strength has to be tested, not assumed.

figure.alt: A printed scrap dipped in sixty degree water goes soft at PLA's glass transition point. A car dashboard in direct sun can pass seventy degrees, well above that line, which is why a printed bracket left there can warp.

steps.title: Why a printed part goes soft in a hot car
steps.body:
PLA, the plastic your printer melts and extrudes, does not stay rigid forever. Around 60 C it crosses what materials scientists call its glass transition, the point where hard plastic turns rubbery and sags under its own weight.

Sixty degrees sounds high, but a car dashboard in direct sun can pass 70 C on a warm day, well past that line. A bracket that holds a phone perfectly on your desk can warp flat on a dashboard by afternoon.

Try it with the kit's thermometer, an adult nearby. Warm a cup of water until it reads 60 C. Use tongs, not fingers, to dip a spare printed scrap in for thirty seconds. Bend it gently afterward. It should flex where the same piece would stay stiff at room temperature.

Nothing broke. The plastic simply crossed its glass transition and came back once it cooled. That is also why filament, and finished prints, should never sit on a sunny windowsill.

figure.alt: The printed part rests on two stands near its ends, with a paper cup hanging by a string from its middle. Washers are added to the cup one at a time to load the part until it flexes or breaks.

steps.title: Print three infill settings, then test to failure
steps.body:
Model the part in Tinkercad to the measurements from the plan and export it once. Print the same file three times with three different infill settings, for example 10 percent, 30 percent and 50 percent. Change nothing else about the print, and note the print time the slicer software reports for each one.

With an adult present, since a snapping part can fling small pieces, run the same strength test on all three once each piece has cooled. Support the part the same way each time and hang a small paper cup from its middle or its weakest-looking point. Add washers or pennies one at a time until it visibly flexes a lot or breaks. Count how many grams it held right before that happened.

Each test destroys that piece, so there is only one honest run per setting. Keep the shape, the support method and how the weight is added exactly the same across all three so the comparison is fair.

Finish by printing a second version of your working part at whichever infill actually held up, and fit it to the mBot.
checklist: The same part shape was printed at three different infill settings, nothing else changed
Print time was recorded for each of the three settings
Each piece was loaded the same way until it flexed a lot or broke, and the failure weight recorded
A second, improved version of the part was printed and fits the mBot

steps.title: Infill versus print time and strength
steps.body:
The part's shape, the support method and how weight was added stay the same for all three rows. Only the infill percentage changes, and each piece is tested to failure only once since the test destroys it.

Three rows, one per infill setting. For each row, write the infill percentage, the print time in minutes, and the weight in grams the part held right before it flexed a lot or broke.
steps.question: Which infill percentage held the most weight, and how many more minutes did it take to print than the lowest infill?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: a part that does not fit the mBot's screw holes because a measurement was off by a millimetre or two.

Also watch for a low-infill piece that flexes so easily the failure point is hard to pin down. And a print that warps or lifts off the bed partway through.
